justification: Target query: "how to calculate time complexity" (CONTENT_PLAN.md §7.1 row 2). WebSearch was unavailable this session (session budget exhausted), so I read three of the pages round 1 already identified as ranking for this query and adjacent phrasing directly via WebFetch: GeeksforGeeks's 'how to analyse loops' page, its 'analysis of loops' set-4 page, and freeCodeCamp's introductory piece. All three stop at loop-shape complexity (constant/linear/quadratic/log/log-log, consecutive-loop summing); none covers dependent-bound (triangular) loops with a derived closed form, recursion trees, recurrence relations, the Master Theorem in any of its three cases, the regularity condition, or when the theorem fails to apply (subtractive recurrences, unequal subproblems, the case-2/3 gap) — freeCodeCamp has no recursion coverage at all. This article covers all of that, every claim backed by an instrumented C# program whose measured counts match the derived closed form, plus a five-step procedure at the end that is a genuine synthesis, not a rehash of headings. That is a real, verified content gap the top-ranking pages leave open, and it is delivered with a working-code standard those pages do not meet. Structurally it earns its assigned Q shape (every heading a real search-style question) and stays clearly distinct from the declarative-heading sibling complexity/big-o-notation.md, whose loop coverage it explicitly builds on rather than repeats (confirmed by rereading big-o-notation.md: it stops at a single loop and one pair of independent nested loops, never touches dependent bounds, recursion trees or recurrences). Its own analogies (warehouse stock check, round-robin tournament, halving pallet, leaderboard max/merge/cross-pairs) do not reuse any example from the compared pages or from the sibling article, and none of five spot-checked distinctive sentences turned up as a copy or close paraphrase elsewhere. No filler intro/outro, no keyword stuffing, exercises vary in form and keep their output panels inside the collapsed solution. docs/crosslinks/complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md exists and documents sensible boundaries with the three unpublished siblings it would otherwise link to, so the missing body links are not held against it, and the one live cross-link (/algorithms/binary-search/) resolves to a published article — no dead ends found. This is round 2. I formed the above independently, then opened the round-1 review (8.8) and re-checked its one major and two minor findings against the current text and the git diff between the round-1 and round-2 commits: (1) the major finding — CLRS chapter 4 was cited but chapter 7 (Quicksort), also listed in front matter, was never cited inline — is fixed: the quicksort-worst-case paragraph now reads '...the degenerate case CLRS chapter 7 walks through for exactly this pivot choice,' a genuine inline citation, not decoration. (2) The '1 megabyte' minor is fixed: the phrase is now hyperlinked to the Thread constructor source, matching how the adjacent StackOverflowException claim is linked. (3) The Karatsuba-sourcing minor is only half-fixed: the writer removed the named claim ('Karatsuba's integer multiplication algorithm') rather than sourcing it, replacing it with an anonymized description of the same technique ('a real technique for multiplying large integers... combine three half-size multiplications with extra additions instead'). That still asserts a specific, non-obvious factual claim — a real algorithm exists that beats naive four-multiplication splitting via this exact recurrence shape — with no source anywhere in front matter or inline, so the underlying hard-rule-3 gap from round 1 persists in a harder-to-verify form; this keeps the article from the very top of the scale. I also noticed, as a secondary finding not present in round 1's AdSense review, that the same round-2 edit that fixed the CLRS-chapter-7 gap also corrected a stack-depth error the technical critic had flagged as a blocker (the :::dotnet callout no longer claims RecursiveMax allocates Θ(n) frames); that is not an AdSense-scope finding, but it means no other regression was introduced by the round-2 pass. Net: two of three round-1 sourcing gaps are genuinely closed and the content advantage over the top-ranking results is larger than round 1 already found, which is why the score moves up from 8.8, not because effort was spent but because the article, read fresh today, is measurably better and has only one lingering minor.

issues.problem: This is the round-2 rewrite of the round-1 Karatsuba passage. The specific algorithm name was removed, but the underlying non-obvious factual claim was not: it still asserts that a real, named technique exists that solves T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) by trading one multiplication for extra additions and beats the naive four-multiplication split for large n. No source for this claim appears in front matter or inline, unlike every other named technique/result in the article (merge sort, quicksort, binary search, Array.Sort are all sourced). Per hard rule 3, a non-obvious factual claim needs a primary source fetched and read during research; anonymizing the claim does not exempt it.
